text: General dietary guidance for people at risk of or living with type-2 diabetes: limit sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates, prioritize vegetables and fiber-rich foods, and keep portion sizes for staples like rice consistent across meals. This is general education, not a personal diet plan; a doctor or registered dietitian should set individual targets.

Regular physical activity, such as brisk walking for at least 150 minutes per week, is commonly recommended as part of type-2 diabetes prevention and management because it improves insulin sensitivity. People with existing heart, joint, or eye complications should check with a doctor before starting a new routine.
source_name: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes

text: Common symptoms associated with high blood glucose include excessive thirst, frequent urination, unexplained fatigue, blurred vision, and slow-healing wounds. Symptoms alone cannot confirm diabetes; a clinical blood test is required for diagnosis.

Medication and insulin decisions, including starting, stopping, or adjusting a dose, must be made by a qualified doctor based on clinical tests and full medical history. This system cannot and does not prescribe, recommend, or adjust medication.

Diabetes is clinically confirmed using tests such as fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, or an oral glucose tolerance test, interpreted by a healthcare professional. A statistical risk estimate from this prototype is a prompt to seek testing, not a diagnosis.

Recognized risk factors for type-2 diabetes include higher body mass index, elevated blood pressure, a family history of diabetes, older age, and low physical activity. Having one or more risk factors raises statistical likelihood; it does not guarantee the condition will develop.

Poorly controlled diabetes over time is associated with complications affecting the eyes, kidneys, nerves, feet, and cardiovascular system. Regular checkups and early management substantially reduce this risk.

South Asian populations, including Bangladesh, show a pattern of higher diabetes risk at lower body mass index thresholds than Western populations, which is one reason population-specific screening data is valuable rather than relying only on global cutoffs.
